title: The Stability of Online Algorithms in Performative Prediction
claim: A feedback loop between deployed models and induced data defines stability: no alternative model beats the randomized deployed mixture in hindsight.
layout: 2 panels, left cycle diagram then right definition box, math-heavy callout
description: The figure has two parts. On the left, three rounded boxes are connected by curved and straight arrows in a cycle. The top box reads 'Model influences data z_t ~ D(θ_t)'. An arrow leads down to the lower-right box 'Loss ℓ(z_t; θ_t) is incurred'. An arrow then leads left to 'Learner samples model θ_t ~ μ_PS', and a final arrow goes back up to the top box. This shows the performative feedback loop. On the right, a light-blue rounded box states the definition informally. The mixture μ_PS is ε-performatively stable if, in expectation, the average loss of the deployed models over t=1..n is at most the average loss of any fixed alternative θ'. A sentence below says no other model has lower loss on the data the mixture induces. The figure is black and white apart from the blue box. The eye goes first to the cycle, then to the inequality.
caption: Visualizing the performative stability guarantee. A mixture $\mu$ over models $\theta$ is stable if it shapes the data in a way that its own predictions are risk minimizing. Our notion, [ref], generalizes the prior notion where $\mu$ is a point mass on a single model.
abstract: The use of algorithmic predictions in decision-making leads to a feedback loop where the models we deploy actively influence the data distributions we see, and later use to retrain on. This dynamic was formalized by Perdomo et al. 2020 in their work on performative prediction. Our main result is an unconditional reduction showing that any no-regret algorithm deployed in performative settings converges to a (mixed) performatively stable equilibrium: a solution in which models actively shape data distributions in ways that their own predictions look optimal in hindsight. Prior to our work, all positive results in this area imposed strong restrictions on how models influenced distributions. By using a martingale argument and allowing randomization, we avoid any assumption on how populations respond to predictions and sidestep recent hardness results showing that deterministic stable models are in general PPAD-hard to compute. Lastly, on a more conceptual note, our connection sheds light on why common algorithms, like gradient descent, are naturally stabilizing and prevent runaway feedback loops. We hope our work enables future technical transfer of ideas between online optimization and performativity.
